transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

Report PR-AUC as your main number, and add ROC-AUC only as secondary context. **Why:** when churners are this rare, ROC-AUC can look strong even when many of your churn flags are wrong. ROC uses the false-positive rate, and that rate stays small because there are so many non-churners. PR-AUC uses precision, so it shows how many of the customers you flag actually churn. That is what a retention budget depends on. **To make it concrete for your manager:**
- Give the baseline. A random model's PR-AUC equals the share of churners, which is your 3%. Say how far above that you are. - Add precision and recall at the cut-off you would actually use, for example the riskiest slice of customers you could afford to contact. That answer is complete, and no data work is needed. Is there anything else you'd like me to expand on, such as how to word this for your manager?
ok that's the answer i expected. i don't need the wording help. just confirm one thing: is there any case where roc-auc should be the headline instead? if no, we're done.

Yes, there are a few cases. ROC-AUC should be the headline when:
- You need a score that doesn't depend on the base rate. This applies when you compare models or segments with different churn rates, or when the churn rate will shift between training and deployment. ROC-AUC doesn't change with prevalence, but PR-AUC does. - You care about ranking both classes well, and false positives and false negatives matter about equally. - Your audience already uses ROC-AUC as the standard, and you are tracking the same metric over time. For a 3% churn problem where you contact the top-risk customers, none of these usually applies, so PR-AUC stays the headline. Does that settle it?

Does that settle it, or is there a case you're weighing where the base rate might shift?
Yes, that settles it. PR-AUC as headline, ROC-AUC secondary. We're done.
Good, PR-AUC as the headline and ROC-AUC as secondary context. Good luck with your manager.

transcript.text: people say AI can predict no-shows. is that real or hype?

It's real, but how well it works depends on your situation. Models can usually rank appointments by how likely they are to be missed, especially when you have a history of past bookings and outcomes. They can't tell you which individual will skip, and they only help if you act on the ranking, for example with reminders or smart overbooking. What's behind your question? Do you run something where no-shows cost you, or are you just curious?

Yes, we run a dental clinic in Melbourne with 3 dentists. No-shows cost us money pretty much every week. I'm wondering if predicting them is realistic for a clinic our size, or if it's just a fancy thing for big companies.

Realistic, yes, for a clinic your size, as long as you have enough history. Three dentists usually means a few thousand appointments over a couple of years, which can be enough for a useful ranking, though not a precise one. Does your booking system record past appointments with whether each patient attended or not, and roughly how far back does it go?
Booking software has about 2 years of appointments, I think. I haven't pulled anything out of it yet. I'm not sure if it marks who turned up and who didn't, honestly.

That's fine, it's the one thing we need to find out first. Most booking systems have a status per appointment, like "attended", "cancelled" or "DNA" (did not attend). Could you ask your software provider, or look at an appointment report, and tell me whether no-shows are marked that way? Then we can pull an export together.

Not sure, to be honest. I'd have to check. I think there's a report somewhere but I don't know how to find it. Is it something my receptionist could sort out, or do I need to ring the software company? I'm also still trying to work out whether this is worth a few thousand dollars or whether I should just send more reminder texts.

Start with your receptionist. She probably knows the software best, so ask her for an appointment list for the last 2 years that shows each appointment's status (attended, cancelled, DNA), exported to Excel or CSV. If she can't find it, ring the software company. Meanwhile, you're right to weigh reminders against prediction, because reminders are the cheap first move. Do you already text reminders to every patient, and when do they go out?

Um, I think the software sends some kind of reminder text, maybe a day before? Not sure about the timing or if it goes to everyone. My receptionist would know. So should I get her to do the export first, or is there a cheaper way to test this before paying anyone?

Yes, the export first. It costs nothing, and it's also the cheapest test. Ask your receptionist for 2 years of appointments with date, dentist, appointment type, and status (attended, cancelled, DNA). Once you share that, I can work out your real no-show rate and whether it clusters, for example by day, dentist or new patients. That will show whether prediction could beat simply changing your reminders. Roughly how many no-shows do you think you get in a typical week, and what does an empty slot cost you?

Hmm, I'd guess maybe five or six a week? Hard to say exactly. An empty slot is probably a couple hundred dollars once you count the chair time, but I'd have to check with my accountant. I don't really know what a model would cost, that's part of why I'm asking.

Those guesses are enough for a first estimate. That's the most a perfect fix could save you, and no model gets close to perfect. So your cost matters more than any model's price. If reminders alone recover even a third of that, prediction may not be worth buying yet. Your export will show whether no-shows cluster enough to target. Could you ask your receptionist to pull it this week, and also tell you when the reminder texts go out and to whom?

Ok, I'll ask her to pull it this week and find out about the reminders. Honestly I don't know what a freelancer would charge for something like this. Is a few thousand dollars normal for that, or would it be way more?

I can't give you a reliable freelancer price, and I'd rather not guess. A few thousand dollars may be plausible for a small one-off model, but quotes vary a lot. Get two or three, and ask what's included. Your own numbers are the better guide. You said you lose five or six appointments a week, and that each empty slot costs "a couple hundred dollars". That's the most a perfect fix could save you. A model would recover only part of it, and only if you act on its predictions. Once your export shows your real no-show rate, we can judge whether a few thousand dollars is worth it. If it isn't, better reminders are the cheaper move. Next, you ask your receptionist for the export and for the reminder details: when the texts go out and to whom. When you share the table, I'll check whether no-shows cluster by day, dentist or patient type. Until then, there's nothing to buy.
